And I'll be straight with you - when I see someone who's clearly struggling with drinking or drugs right here where kids are playing, that bothers me. Not because I think I'm better than anyone, but because this used to be the kind of place where that stuff stayed behind closed doors. Now it feels like anything goes, and I'm not sure that's progress.

I try to be polite, wave hello and all that. But real connection? That takes more than just good intentions. It takes understanding how this place works, respecting what people have built here over time. Some folks get that, others... well, they seem to think everything should just change to accommodate them.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
*shifts uncomfortably, then leans forward with a serious expression*

Look, I'm not trying to be the morality police here, but there's a difference between tolerance and just letting everything slide, you know? 

With the drinking and drug stuff - that's not about judging people, that's about safety. I've got nephews who play in this neighborhood. When someone's stumbling around drunk at two in the afternoon or leaving needles where kids might find them, that's not a lifestyle choice anymore - that's a problem that affects all of us. I'd rather have an honest conversation about getting help than just pretend it's not happening.

The disease thing... hell, that's tough. I mean, if someone's got something contagious, don't we have a right to know? Not to shun them, but to protect ourselves and our families? My mom's got diabetes, her immune system isn't great. I'm not saying people should be outcasts, but there's got to be some common sense here.

As for the other stuff - different races, religions, whatever - I don't really care what color someone is or what they believe as long as they're decent people. But the language barrier, that's real. How are we supposed to build community when we can't even talk to each other? Maybe I'm old-fashioned, but if you're going to live somewhere, shouldn't you at least try to learn how to communicate with your neighbors?

And the unmarried couples thing... look, I was raised a certain way, but that's not really my business. What bothers me more is when people act like the way I was raised is automatically wrong or outdated. There's room for different ways of living, but it should go both ways, right?

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character13_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*rubs jaw thoughtfully, voice getting more intense*

Now that's hitting close to home. You want to know about fairness? Fair is when the guy who's been paying into the system his whole life gets first crack at the job, not last.

I've been looking for steady work for eight months now. Eight months. And I keep hearing about how there's plenty of jobs, but then I go apply and they tell me the position's been filled, or they're "looking for someone with different qualifications." Meanwhile, I drive by construction sites and hear more Spanish than English. I'm not saying those guys don't work hard - they do. But what about the rest of us?

My buddy Mike, he's got fifteen years experience in roofing, and he's competing with guys who'll do the same job for half the pay and no benefits. How's that fair to Mike? How's that fair to his kids who need health insurance? These companies, they love it because it keeps their costs down, but what happens to the community when the people who built it can't afford to live in it anymore?

Look, I get that people are trying to make a better life for themselves - I respect that. But there's got to be some kind of order to this. Americans first, right? People who've been paying taxes, following the rules, waiting their turn. If there's work left over after that, fine. But when my neighbor can't feed his family because someone else will work for peanuts, that's not fairness - that's just cheap labor with a fancy name.

And don't get me started on all the programs and services going to people who just got here while guys like me can't even get unemployment extended. That's not the America I grew up believing in.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character13_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*takes a deep breath, looking thoughtful but frustrated*

Alright, let me break this down how I see it.

The labor shortage thing - yeah, I keep hearing that, but where are these shortages? Because I'm not seeing them where I live. Maybe in some fancy tech jobs or whatever, but for regular working folks? Come on. If there was really a shortage of workers, wages would be going up, not staying flat while everything else costs more.

Cultural diversity and vitality - look, I'm not against people having their own traditions, but let's be real about what that means on the ground. When half the signs in my town are in a language I can't read, when my kid comes home from school talking about holidays I've never heard of being treated like they're more important than the ones we grew up with... that doesn't feel like diversity, it feels like replacement.

Security concerns? Hell yes, that's reasonable. We don't even know who's coming in half the time. I'm not saying everyone's a terrorist, but we've got a right to know who's in our country. When I apply for a job, they do a background check. When someone wants to become my neighbor permanently, shouldn't we at least do the same?

The humanitarian stuff... look, I feel bad for people in tough situations, I really do. But we've got our own people sleeping on the streets, our own veterans who can't get help, our own kids in failing schools. Charity starts at home, doesn't it? How can we save the world when we can't even take care of our own?

The employment impact - that's not a fear, that's reality. I'm living it. Anyone who says immigration doesn't affect wages and jobs either doesn't work with their hands or is lying.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character13_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*leans back, speaking with conviction*

Complete openness? That's just insane. No country in the world does that because it doesn't work. You'd have chaos - complete chaos. Infrastructure would collapse, wages would tank, and you'd have people flooding in faster than anyone could handle. That's not policy, that's just wishful thinking.

The job demand thing sounds reasonable on paper, but who's deciding what jobs we "need" filled? The same companies that want cheap labor? The same politicians who don't live in neighborhoods like mine? I don't trust that system because it's rigged from the start.

Here's what makes sense to me: strict numerical limits, and I mean strict. Maybe 100,000 people a year, tops. And it should be based on what Americans need, not what businesses want. First priority goes to people with skills we actually can't find here - and I mean really can't find, not just "can't find at the price we want to pay."

But here's the key - anyone who comes here has to prove they can integrate. Learn English within two years, no exceptions. Pass a civics test that shows they understand American values and history. No criminal record, clean health screening, and they have to have a job lined up that pays at least the local average wage - none of this undercutting American workers stuff.

And if you're here illegally? You go to the back of the line, period. We can't reward people for breaking the rules while others wait years doing it the right way.

Most importantly - we take care of our own first. Every homeless veteran housed, every American who wants work has work, every kid in a decent school. Then we can talk about helping others. That's not heartless, that's just common sense.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character13_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character13_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*pauses, then speaks more softly, as J stepping back from the role*

You know... that was harder than I expected. Really getting into his headspace like that - I could feel how real those concerns were for him. The frustration, the sense that the world was changing around him faster than he could keep up with.

What struck me most was how much of his views came from genuine experiences - watching his dad work hard his whole life, seeing his buddy Mike struggle to find work, living in a community where he felt like the rules kept changing. It wasn't just abstract politics for him; it was personal. Very personal.

I think I understand now why he got so heated about these topics. When you're already struggling and then you feel like the system is working against you... I can see how that would build up. He wasn't just angry at immigrants - he was angry at feeling powerless, at watching his version of the American dream slip away.

As for my own views... honestly, it's complicated. I still don't agree with all his positions, but I get the human side of it better now. The fear isn't always about hatred - sometimes it's about survival, about protecting what little stability you have. That doesn't make every viewpoint right, but it makes the person behind those views more... understandable.

I miss him, you know? Even when we disagreed about this stuff. He cared deeply about fairness and community, even if we defined those things differently. Playing his role reminded me that behind every political opinion is usually someone just trying to make sense of their world and protect the people they love.

*looks thoughtful* Maybe that's what we're missing in these conversations - remembering the person behind the politics.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character13_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Yeah… fairness, belonging, community — those weren’t just words to him. They were real, like something you could feel in your gut. He always said fairness meant everybody gettin’ a shot — not the same thing, but a *fair* chance. Like, if you’re workin’ hard, showin’ up every day, tryin’ to do right by your family, then you shouldn’t get stepped on just ‘cause someone’s got more connections or money.

He grew up seein’ folks fall through the cracks. His old man worked the line at a plant for twenty years, came home exhausted every night, and still barely made enough to keep the lights on. When the plant shut down, nobody came to help — not really. The company moved out, politicians gave speeches, but nothin’ changed for people like them. That stuck with him. So when he talked about fairness, it wasn’t abstract. It was about dignity. About not bein’ forgotten.

Belonging? That mattered a lot. He didn’t go to college, so his world was mostly here — this town, this neighborhood, the guys he worked with, the barbershop, the VFW hall. He felt rooted. But he also knew what it was like to feel invisible, like when outsiders looked at places like ours and called us “flyover country” or “left behind.” That pissed him off. Not because he hated others, but ‘cause it made people feel like they didn’t matter. Belonging, to him, meant bein’ seen. Bein’ respected. Knowin’ your life counts.

Community, he used to say, wasn’t just geography. It was trust. It was lookin’ out for each other. He remembered how folks came together after the flood back in ’18 — sandbaggin’ all night, openin’ up homes to strangers. Didn’t matter who you were; if you needed help, you got it. But he also worried that we were losin’ that. That things were changin’ fast — jobs gone, people movin’ in and out, different languages, new ways of livin’. Not all bad, but… it made some folks uneasy. Including him sometimes.

He wasn’t against change. But he wanted it to include people like him — not just replace them.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character13_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Yeah, I’m sittin’ here on this old bench in the garden, sun’s comin’ through the trees, kids laughin’ over by the compost bins. You see all kinds of folks now — wasn’t always like that.

Used to be, most people around here were like me — grew up in town, worked at the mill or the garage, went to church on Sundays whether they believed it or not. Now? There’s Maria and her boys from Guatemala down the street — she works two jobs, runs a little cleaning business. Then there’s Mr. Kim, fixes appliances outta his garage, quiet guy, real careful with his tools. And across the alley, Jamal and his wife — he’s from Sudan, works nights at the hospital. Their daughter just started school this year.

I’ll be honest — at first, I didn’t know how to talk to some of ‘em. Different ways, different customs. Felt awkward. Like we were passin’ each other in silence, both wonderin’ what the other thinks. But then one day, I helped Mr. Kim carry a fridge back from the dump, and he brought me a jar of kimchi next week — said his wife made it. Tasted like fire and vinegar, but I ate every bite ‘cause it meant somethin’. He smiled — first time I’d seen him do that.

So yeah, it’s different now. Some folks grumble — say “we’re losin’ the character of the neighborhood.” But I think the character *is* changin’, and maybe that’s okay, as long as we’re still treatin’ each other right.

I’ve seen folks help each other — when Jamal’s car broke down in winter, Frank from three doors down — old Army guy, used to mutter about “them outsiders” — he towed it home and fixed the starter. Didn’t charge nothin’.

But… I also see the hard parts. There’s that guy near the bus stop — drinks all day, sleeps under the bridge sometimes. People say he’s got PTSD from Iraq, but nobody really checks on him. And there’s others — young ones, caught up in pills, can’t hold jobs. Doesn’t matter where you’re from — white, brown, whatever — pain looks the same when you’re starin’ into nothing.

And yeah, some new families come in, and sure, there’s language barriers, different beliefs. Some go to mosques, some don’t believe in God at all. Others live together without bein’ married — used to make me side-eye ‘em, but then I thought… hell, my sister’s been with her man ten years, no ring, raise two good kids. Who am I to judge?

What matters is: are you decent? Do you keep your yard clean? Say hello? Help if someone’s hurt?

That’s what belonging means here now, I think. Not everybody has to be the same. But we gotta meet in the middle. Can’t expect folks to erase who they are — but also can’t just walk in and act like the people already here don’t count.

The garden helps. We grow food together. Same dirt under everyone’s nails. That’s real. That’s fair.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Yeah… you look around this garden, and you see it all. The guy who talks to himself while pullin’ weeds — been that way since he came back from Afghanistan. The young couple — both women — livin’ in the blue house, tryin’ to adopt a kid. Mrs. Lin from down the block, wearin’ her hijab, prayin’ on a mat out back like clockwork every afternoon. And then there’s people like Randy — used to work construction with me — now can’t go a day without oxy or whatever’s floatin’ through.

Point is, we’re all here. Together. And comfort? That don’t come automatic. It comes from knowin’ someone sees you — not just tolerates you, but *sees* you.

I’ll admit — some things threw me at first. When I heard about the two women wantin’ to start a family, my gut said, “That ain’t natural.” But then I watched ‘em fix up their porch, plant flowers, wave at kids walkin’ to school. They pay taxes. They shovel snow for old Mrs. Gable next door. One night, when she fell, they were the ones called 911 and stayed till the ambulance came.

So I had to ask myself: what’s more important — how they love, or how they live?

Same with religion. Didn’t know much about Islam till Mr. Kim started talkin’. Turns out, he prays five times a day ‘cause it keeps him grounded. Said it’s no different than me kneelin’ at church when my dad died. Both of us askin’ for strength. Took me a minute to get that. But once I did, it made sense.

Now, the hard part — the addiction, the mental stuff — that’s where patience wears thin. Not ‘cause we don’t care, but ‘cause it feels hopeless sometimes. Like Randy — good worker, funny guy, could fix any machine. Now he steals tools just to feed his habit. Last week, he took a trowel right outta the garden shed. Kid caught him. Wasn’t proud.

But then the clinic set up that mobile van — the one with the nurse who knows harm reduction? They got Randy on a program. Not perfect, but he’s showin’ up again. Starts talkin’ to people. You gotta have systems in place — not just judgment.

And diseases — yeah, some folks worry. HIV, hepatitis — especially with needles poppin’ up near the playground. Fear’s real. But fear shouldn’t shut down compassion. We put up sharps boxes, started clean-up days. Education helps. One of the outreach workers — Latina woman, sharp as hell — sat us all down, explained how you *don’t* catch stuff just by bein’ near someone. Changed minds.

Communication’s the key. Not preachin’. Not arguin’. Just sittin’ down, side by side, like we are now, and sayin’: *This is who I am. This is what I need. What about you?*

Tolerance? Yeah, we need more of it — especially when it’s uncomfortable. But tolerance ain’t enough. We need *respect*. Even if we don’t understand. Especially then.

Reason I push for that? ‘Cause I’ve seen what happens when we don’t — towns tearin’ apart, people isolated, dyin’ alone. My dad never asked for help when he was hurtin’. Thought men didn’t do that. Ended up bitter. Don’t want that for anyone else.

So yeah, we make space. Not because it’s easy. But because community means nobody gets left behind — no matter their past, their body, who they love, or where they’re from. We figure it out together. That’s what belonging *should* mean.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character13_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Fairness, when jobs are tight? That’s the real test.

Look — I believe people should earn their way. No handouts. But also no rigged game. When work’s scarce, fairness means the guy who’s been payin’ taxes here for twenty years, raisin’ kids in this town, shouldn’t be passed over for someone flown in from somewhere else just ‘cause he’s cheaper labor or easier to push around.

I’ve seen it happen. The chicken plant out near Route 9? Used to hire locals. Union wages, decent hours. Then they brought in a crew — mostly immigrants, some legal, some not — housed ‘em in trailers, paid less, worked ‘em longer. Bosses said they were “filling positions Americans won’t take.” But that ain’t true. *We* would’ve taken ‘em — if they’d paid livable wages and treated folks right.

So when resources are tight, fairness means protecting opportunity for *everyone*, but especially those already rooted here — people with families in the schools, houses they’re tryin’ to keep, bills piling up. You don’t shut the door on newcomers, but you don’t throw your own people under the bus neither.

Migrant workers — yeah, some of ‘em are hard workers. Hell, my cousin works alongside a Guatemalan crew on a roofing team. Says they show up early, stay late, don’t complain. He respects ‘em. But he also says the contractor uses ‘em to break bids — undercut local crews who can’t compete with $12-an-hour cash jobs and no benefits.

That ain’t fair to anybody. Not to us, not to them — ‘cause they get exploited too.

So balance? It’s gotta be based on rules. If a job opens up, give locals first shot — especially if they’ve got skills, experience, need the work. If nobody’s qualified or willing after a real effort to hire? Then bring someone in. But make sure they’re legal, payin’ taxes, playin’ by the same rules. No backdoor deals.

And while we’re at it — invest in training. Too many guys like me, stuck with a high school diploma, feel left behind. Offer apprenticeships, trade programs, help people adapt. Don’t just say “go back to school” when tuition costs more than a house.

Also — stop treatin’ immigration like it’s only about economics. It’s about people. There’s refugees — folks runnin’ from war, gangs, hell — they deserve a chance. But we can’t pretend we’ve got infinite capacity. Our hospitals are strained, our schools understaffed, housing’s tight. Compassion’s important, but so’s order.

Fairness means: if you come here, do it right. Wait your turn. Respect the process. And while you’re waitin’, we’ll make sure the people already standin’ in line — the ones born here, raised here, fightin’ to survive — don’t get shoved aside.

Because when jobs disappear and folks feel replaced — not by better ideas, but by cheaper bodies — that’s when bitterness grows. That’s when neighbors stop trustin’ each other. That’s when community breaks.

I want a country big enough for all of us. But it’s gotta be fair. Not just on paper — in practice. For everyone. Local or new. White, brown, doesn’t matter. But you can’t talk about fairness without talkin’ about dignity — and dignity means knowin’ your life still matters in your own hometown.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character13_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
You ask about the big picture — national level — and yeah, it’s messy. A lot of noise, a lot of fear, a lot of pride. But when I think about it, not all the views out there are wrong. Some just come from different kinds of pain.

First off — *yes*, immigrants fill jobs people won’t take. That part? I can’t deny it. I’ve seen farms outside the county where no one local wants to bend over in the heat for twelve hours picking peppers. Trucking companies say they can’t find drivers. Meatpacking plants? Half the workers are foreign-born. So if the work’s hard, dangerous, or pays too little for Americans to stick around — then sure, newcomers step in. That helps keep food on shelves, trucks movin’. Reasonable point.

And the cultural stuff — the food, the music, the festivals down in the city? I’ll admit, I didn’t get it at first. Felt like another world. But then I went to that Diwali thing last fall with my nephew — lights everywhere, kids laughin’, spices in the air — and damn, it was alive. You feel energy like that, you start seein’ it ain’t about replacin’ us — it’s about addin’ to what we are. So diversity bringin’ vitality? Yeah, that’s real too. Makes places feel less dead.

But then you got the other side — security. Now, I don’t buy that most immigrants are criminals. That’s junk talk, usually pushed by guys yellin’ on TV. Most of ‘em I’ve met are tryin’ to survive, same as us. But — and this is a *but* — I’ve also seen what happens when borders are loose and towns get overwhelmed overnight. Thirty families dropped into a shelter with no plan, no support, some with gang ties or untreated mental illness. One kid got jumped near the high school — turned out he was trafficked, wasn’t even legal. That scared people. Not because he was brown or foreign — but because nobody knew he was comin’, nobody checked.

So when folks talk about crime or terrorism risks — I don’t think they’re all racists. Some are just scared of chaos. Of not knowin’ who’s here, why they came, or if systems can handle it. Fear of the unknown — that’s human. Doesn’t make it right every time, but it’s real.

Humanitarian side — refugees, people runnin’ from war, poverty — that hits me deep. My granddad came over from Ireland after the famine. No money, no English, slept in a warehouse. But someone gave him a chance. So if we can help a Syrian mom with three kids escape a bombed-out city? Hell yes. If we can save a Honduran teen from being forced into a gang? Absolutely.

But — again — capacity matters. We can’t be blind to our own. I drive past tent cities every day. Veterans sleepin’ under bridges. Kids in foster care. Schools with no books. So when billions go to resettle people from abroad while our own neighborhoods crumble? That feels twisted. Compassion shouldn’t have a passport.

And then there’s the money thing — wages goin’ down, jobs gettin’ harder to find. I’ve sat in union halls and heard guys say, “I bid on that job, offered fair pay — but the contractor hired a crew from outta state, payin’ cash, no benefits.” That ain’t immigration policy — that’s exploitation. But it gets blamed on immigrants anyway. And when wages stagnate for twenty years while CEOs get bonuses, people look around for someone to blame. Sometimes it’s the guy with the accent.

So which views are reasonable?

- **Labor shortages?** Yes — but only if wages reflect true cost of living, and locals aren’t shut out.
- **Cultural vitality?** Yes — but only if integration goes both ways. Don’t expect people to erase their roots, but don’t demand newcomers ignore ours, either.
- **Security concerns?** Some valid — especially around vetting, tracking, and community readiness. But often blown up with lies. Needs facts, not fear.
- **Humanitarian duty?** Yes — we should help those in real danger. But it can’t come at the cost of abandoning our own poor, broken, forgotten.
- **Economic fears?** Absolutely valid. When work disappears and wages drop, it ain’t imaginary. But the real enemy ain’t immigrants — it’s greedy bosses and politicians who let ‘em exploit anyone, citizen or not.

What needs more evidence? The crime stats. I’ve heard both sides — “immigrants commit less crime” and “gangs are crossing the border.” We need straight answers, not slogans. Also — long-term impact on schools, hospitals, housing. Are we planning, or just reactin’?

And dialogue? Hell yes. Not shoutin’ matches on cable news. Real talk — in churches, VFW halls, community centers. Sit a veteran next to a refugee. Let ‘em tell their story. Not to win, but to hear.

Because right now? Too many feel replaced. Too many feel ignored. And that poison spreads fast.

Fairness ain’t about numbers. It’s about respect. For everyone. But you can’t demand loyalty from people whose lives keep gettin’ treated like they don’t count.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character13_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t go for any one of those extremes. Not complete openness — as much as I believe in second chances, we’re not endless. We’ve got schools full, ERs runnin’ on fumes, housing so tight people are livin’ in trailers in the summer heat. You can’t just open the gates and say “come on in” without a plan. That’s not kindness — that’s chaos.

And I’d *definitely* say no to refusin’ all foreign workers. That’s ignorant. We need people — especially in jobs most of us won’t do or can’t fill. Agriculture, nursing homes, construction — you think an old white guy like me wants to gut chickens at 4 a.m. in a freezing plant? No. But someone’s gotta do it. So shuttin’ out all workers? Stupid. Hurts the economy, hurts families who depend on services.

So what do I want?

A mix — **job-based admission with limits, rules, and accountability**.

First: **Admit people based on real job demand**, but only after proving the job *can’t* be filled locally. I mean real proof — not some boss sayin’, “Americans are lazy.” Post the job. Offer fair wages. Give veterans, laid-off workers, people from around here a real shot. If nobody takes it after six weeks? Then bring someone in — legally, through a visa program tied to that job and that job only.

And pay them right. Same wage, same safety rules, same dignity. No undercutting. No cash-in-hand schemes to break unions or lower standards. If we’re gonna hire outsiders, they shouldn’t be used as tools to crush our own people’s pay.

Second: **Set smart numerical limits** — not arbitrary numbers pulled from thin air, but based on what towns like ours can actually absorb. Not just housing, but schools, clinics, cops, social services. Figure it out region by region. Some cities can take more; rural areas might need workers but can’t support big influxes overnight. Be realistic.

Third: **Protect refugees — but vet thoroughly**. If someone’s runnin’ from war or persecution, we’ve got a moral duty. But we also have a duty to keep our communities safe. So strong background checks, health screenings, clear pathways — not dumping people in neighborhoods with no support. Bring ‘em in slowly, with help — language classes, job training, housing aid. Integration matters. Don’t just drop ‘em and walk away.

Fourth: **Crack down on exploitation — on both sides**. No more companies hiring illegal crews to bust wages. Fine ‘em heavy. And no more smugglers or cartels profitin’ off desperate people. Secure the damn border — not with walls alone, but with technology, patrols, and legal ports of entry that work.

And for those already here — undocumented but workin’, payin’ taxes, stayin’ clean? There should be a way forward — after fines, background checks, learnin’ English, waitin’ their turn. Not jumpin’ the line — but earnin’ status over time. Fairness goes both ways.

Balance? It’s about **order with heart**.

I want a country that still feels like home — where my kid can find work, where the neighborhood doesn’t change so fast you don’t recognize it, where folks still look out for each other. But I also want one that doesn’t slam the door on someone tryin’ to do right, just ‘cause they started behind.

Social integration starts with *belonging*, not just presence. So if someone comes here, they should learn the language, respect the laws, contribute. And in return? We treat ‘em like human beings — not criminals, not saints, just people tryin’ to build something.

Fairness means nobody gets forgotten — not the guy born here strugglin’ to survive, and not the one who crossed a desert just to try.

That’s the policy I’d back. Not perfect. But honest. Grounded. Like this garden — you don’t let weeds take over, but you make room for new seeds — if they grow alongside what’s already rooted.

After walkin’ in his boots today, I get it. It wasn’t hate talkin’. It was fear. Not of people — but of bein’ erased. Of workin’ your whole life only to find out your town, your job, your *place* — didn’t need you anymore.

And I realized something: he wasn’t against immigrants. He was against *unfairness*. Against a system that pits poor against poor, citizen against newcomer, while the ones at the top keep winnin’. He wanted dignity — for himself, for his neighbors, yes, but also for the guy pickin’ lettuce under the same sun.

That changed how I see it.

I used to think more open borders were always the moral choice. Still believe in kindness. But now I see — compassion without structure isn’t justice. It’s just another kind of chaos. And folks like him — working class, no degree, stuck in towns the economy forgot — they’re the first to pay when systems break down.

He didn’t want walls everywhere. He wanted rules that made sense. A line you wait in. A chance to speak up before decisions are made. Respect.

And maybe most of all — he wanted to matter. In the conversation. In the country. In the neighborhood garden where everyone’s hands are dirty, but some feel like guests and others feel like owners.

Talkin’ like him today… it softened me. Not on the issues — I still believe we gotta help those runnin’ from hell — but on *how*. Slow. Fair. With care for everyone already here too.

It made me miss him different. Not just as a friend, but as someone who saw the cracks before most of us did. Not because he was smarter — but because he was *on the edge* of things, feelin’ the pressure first.

And now I carry it — not just his words, but his worry. His hope. That we can build somethin’ wide enough for all of us — without losin’ what holds us together.

That’s what he wanted.  
And now? I want it too.
